Patient Autonomy vs Beneficence

Two of the four cardinal principles of medical ethics (Beauchamp & Childress) frequently come into conflict in clinical practice — autonomy (the patient's right to self-determination) and beneficence (the physician's duty to act in the patient's best interest).

Definitions

  • Autonomy — from Greek autos (self) + nomos (law) — the right of a competent patient to make informed decisions about their own body, including the right to refuse any investigation or treatment, even if such refusal may result in harm or death. Respecting autonomy requires informed consent, confidentiality, truth-telling, and respect for advance directives.
  • Beneficence — the obligation of the physician to act in the best interest of the patient, to promote welfare, prevent harm, and remove harm. Includes actions that go beyond duty (supererogation).

Conflict Scenarios

  • Jehovah's Witness refusing blood transfusion — even in life-threatening haemorrhage, a competent adult JW's refusal must be respected. Transfusing against their will constitutes battery.
  • Refusal of life-saving treatment — a competent adult may refuse dialysis, chemotherapy, mechanical ventilation, or surgery. Physician should ensure capacity, explore reasons, correct reversible factors, offer alternatives, document carefully, and respect the decision.
  • Children & immature minors — parents cannot refuse life-saving treatment on religious grounds for a child; courts usually authorise treatment in the "best interests of the child". The child's beneficence overrides parental autonomy.
  • Pregnant woman refusing Caesarean section — a competent pregnant woman's autonomy prevails even if refusal may harm the fetus. Forced intervention is unethical & legally actionable.
  • Psychiatric patient refusing treatment — if lack of capacity (acute psychosis, suicidal intent), Mental Healthcare Act allows involuntary admission & treatment in best interest; review by Mental Health Review Board.
  • Advance directives & living wills — Common Law (Practice and Procedure) and the Supreme Court of India (Common Cause vs Union of India, 2018) recognise the right to die with dignity — passive euthanasia via advance directive is permissible with safeguards.
  • Truth-telling in terminal illness — Indian cultural practice often involves family hiding diagnosis from patient ("collusion") — ethically problematic; patient autonomy demands disclosure unless the patient has explicitly delegated this to family, or disclosure would cause serious harm.
  • Vaccination refusal — individual autonomy vs public-health beneficence (herd immunity); mandatory vaccination policies for school entry & pandemics are an ongoing debate.

Resolution Framework

  1. Assess decision-making capacity (understand, appreciate, reason, communicate choice).
  2. Ensure the patient has all material information (diagnosis, prognosis, alternatives, risks, benefits).
  3. Voluntariness — confirm no coercion from family or physician.
  4. Explore reasons for refusal — fear, misinformation, cultural/religious beliefs, depression.
  5. Involve ethics committee, palliative care, social worker, family meeting.
  6. Document assessment, discussions, decisions, and the patient's signed informed refusal.
  7. Continue to offer alternative options; reassess capacity at intervals.
  8. Never abandon the patient — continue supportive & palliative care.

Indian Context — Legal Framework

  • Constitution Article 21 — Right to Life & Personal Liberty interpreted to include right to refuse treatment.
  • MHA 2017 — supports advance directives for psychiatric care; capacity-based consent.
  • Supreme Court 2018 — passive euthanasia permitted via living will with strict safeguards.
  • MCI Code of Ethics — consent mandatory before any invasive procedure.

Clinical Pearl

When autonomy and beneficence conflict, autonomy usually prevails in a competent adult. The physician's role is to inform, advise, and respect — not to override. Document capacity, consent/refusal, and rationale carefully; offer continued care. When in doubt, consult the hospital ethics committee.
